text: All right, we're going to go ahead and get this meeting of our Information Technology Committee underway. It's a good afternoon to everybody. Several exciting presentations today. Our ITPAC has been working very closely with staff.

We normally would have them here, but evidently they can telework, so they're all not in town. But I know several of them are watching. Before we jump into the presentation, I want to give a warm welcome to Matthew Harrison, our new chief information officer.

I know everybody on the board's had a chance to meet with him, but got some very exciting things underway in a very few short months. But with that, Matt, we're glad to have you here. And what did he just say? Enjoy it while it lasts. Is that what he?
Okay. The honeymoon. Anyway, I want to turn it over to you. And our first president, you want me to introduce our first presentation is on the, on, and I should have started with this.

This is an idea Supervisor Alcorn brought forward, I think, the customer portal. And it's a great one. I'm looking forward to watching this one all the way through to completion. With that, I'm going to turn it over to you. Great. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

So quick agenda. So we're going to talk through the customer portal that we're working on. we'll have a couple IT initiative updates. We're going to have a quick discussion on the joint committee between us and IT here in the county, as well as with the schools, and then we'll do a wrap-up and answer any questions folks may have. So, Mr. Chairman, Mr. Chairman, members of the board, I'm Matt Harrison, the new director of DIT and the CIO. So, I'm going to kick off our

conversation around the Fairfax customer portal, one account, one experience service, and then I'll hand over the discussion to members of my team. So our vision for the customer portal is pretty simple. It's going to provide a single point of access for residents and businesses to interact with government services. Customers will be able to initiate their experience through a web browser at first and over time be able to access the portal on a mobile device through an IVR interaction or a text message. Our ultimate goal is to meet our customers through the channel that they choose

to engage with us. Fundamentally, we want to transform the experience of our customers through simple, seamless, transparent, and frictionless interactions that help them achieve what they need at a time and a place of their choosing. The portal fits neatly into our efforts around digital modernization and the simplification of our systems and workflows. The effort will challenge us to rethink how our business processes, applications, and infrastructure impact our ability to provide world-class services to our customers. And the customer portal will be designed

for all residents across abilities and languages to ensure access and equity for our customers. This will be supported through the work of an AI ethics committee we will establish in 2026. So I'll turn it over to Maura Power.

Maura Power, I am the Chief Technology Officer and Deputy Director. So moving on, you know, the vision that Matt has given us really sets us up to make sure that we're reducing the amount of friction and the amount of limited visibility that exists right now with our customers and how we're engaged.

Right now, things are very fragmented. If you're trying to work with your SAC, register your kids for SAC, you have a different account than you would have if you were to then try and pay your car tax or do some residential permit. So we want to reduce the frustration that our customers and that our clients are having right now. So through that vision that Matt has given us, we are going to make sure that our technology addresses some of these inefficiencies. And we'll do this all while our environment and

our systems maintain security in the utmost standards. So as mentioned, we know why this is a challenge, right? We understand that there's different things and different technologies and portals and systems that have come up over time. We understand why it matters, right? We understand the importance that it has to our community and to our customers. But I think the impact is one of the things that we'll really have to measure and keep track of as we move forward because this type of impact, this type of transformation will really impact the amount of time that people

are spending with us. They're getting to their services faster and, you know, the citizens, the customers, our community base really, they don't care about the administrative silos that we have. They want to get to the services. They want to get to the action item as quickly as possible. So with that, I'm going to turn this over to Anita Rao, our Chief Applications Officer, to talk us through how we're going to do that. Hi, good afternoon. Anita Rao, Chief Applications Officer and Deputy Director in Information Technology. So how do we get to this vision

and to our ideal future state? That is a complex way of getting there, but how do we get there? Our end goal is to enable access to services through a single entry point, basically giving the ability to our public to create one login and be able to seamlessly interact with different agencies and different departments so they don't have to maintain separate accounts.

That's the goal we want to get to. And our roadmap on how we achieve this is structured around the capability maturity model, a model which helps us build, improve, measure our successes, and then improve our performance.

So currently we are in, as Maura pointed out, we do provide all these services, online services, through our website. But however, they are siloed services. So users have to come in and maintain separate accounts. So our first focus is to go to level two, which is to create a unified digital front door for our users.
So we want to, you know, to do all this, we must drive digital modernization across all our systems. So we are able to get all our systems to the same level and move forward with that.

So the first goal for us is to ensure that we have a single entry point to come in. And then on that, we are going to build on having a single sign-on and unified profiles for all the users, which will then build to the next level of case management and providing transparency for users to check status at one site instead of going to different places.

And ultimately, our goal is to get to a more personalized and proactive services by anticipating how users are interacting with us through this journey and how we get there. So this concept, though is simple, is very complex, right?

There are so many complexities in the back end with integrating multiple legacy systems and also trying to, and it requires a lot of coordination and technical depth and planning to make all this happen. So there's a lot of work, though it looks simple. In addition to that, we also have to make sure that we keep our customers as the most important thing, as the primary commitment should be towards them. And that means we also have to kind of develop a

culture and environment where we are encouraging data sharing among departments and who are historically may have operated independently. And also leveraging responsible use of AI, machine learning, and data analytics to deliver smarter services. And we also have to invest in our workforce and help develop new skill sets to support this new environment. And of course, we have to continue to measure the results rigorously and commit to continuous improvement.

And this is an ongoing commitment and cannot stop with a one-time endeavor of this sort. So this goes, leads to our next steps for the first year. So I think it's important to make sure that we have clarity and alignment on the goals we're trying to achieve and a shared understanding of what it's going to take to get us there.

I'm not going to hit on every point on this slide, but there are some key thoughts that I want you to take away from the discussion. First, we need to get the foundation right on this complex effort by having a clear assessment of our current state and how it impacts our customers' ability to interact with us.

This isn't just technical and architecture, this is a business process as well. Engagement with internal and external stakeholders is absolutely essential. Internal engagement focused on business processes and what change is going to mean for the agencies and externally with users of our digital services.

We're going to utilize technology to evaluate customer behavior and help their preferences guide our design. Governance isn't the most exciting thing about creating new services, but it's essential if we're to understand our priorities, deliverables, and provide clear definition of responsibilities and accountability partners.

We started the foundational work to evaluate various platforms, API integrations, security designs, and the upskilling of our staff. Further, we're going to hire an expert in user-centric design principles to ensure that we're always putting the customer's experience first.

As we stand up our data lake, we will develop data standards, privacy policies, and work with agency partners to create data sharing agreements. Without a commitment to collaborate on this critical work, we are not going to be successful. And lastly, we must deliver.

Our plan in calendar year 2026 is to integrate with two to three key systems, test and launch version one of the self-service portal, available through a web browser, no later than fourth quarter 2026. The customer portal is going to be a recurring topic in these meetings, as long as the chairman agrees to that.

And I look forward to providing updates as we go into next year. So thank you, and we're happy to take any questions you have. All right. I'm going to start with just a couple of quick comments, and I appreciate the customer focus.

I mean, this is not often we focus on requirements a lot of times, but we don't focus enough on service and customer focus. meeting residents expectation but the one that I didn't think you hit hard enough is the security challenges on this just you know we have so much PII personally identified and we need to protect that that makes your job that much harder it's not as easy this thing isn't as you said this isn't as easy as it sounds right but I think uh starting with small good achievable goals and then

working our way through this is the right way to go, so thank you, but it is a monumental feat to pull these disparate systems together and still secure information and everything else that needs to be done. Go ahead. I'm just going to respond to your comment question that we do have security by design principles, so in everything we're doing, we have an outstanding security team, as you know, and leadership there, so this will absolutely be first and foremost in the work that we're doing. Mr. Chairman. Yeah, I love this. I think it's important. I love the timeline.

I realize the complexity, but I think it's also important to point out the efficiencies within county that we get out of this as well. I mean, I can't imagine how much time our staff spends maintaining all these different systems, the clunkiness of them, or absence of a system, having to answer questions and administer things that could be done so much easier by our residents and can be done 24-7. I have to do it during the hours the county is open, and I'm thinking about looking at Jay, and I'm thinking about the portal people use for paying their car

taxes. It's great. You can go on there. You can see all your property. You can verify it. You can click on it. You can change things with it, but I also know it's clunky, and it needs some sophistication, but it saves Jay's folks an immeasurable amount of time where people can be empowered to do the things they need to do on their schedule at home helps the customer helps the county and so I just want to underscore the work that's being put into this and the resources needed to do this are so worth it for both of those reasons and so I'm excited about this I

guess the challenge that's ahead of us and it may be too early to know this is we have a lot of what I would call oddities so we have county agencies obviously this should be an all-county hands-on deck exercise. But then we have the park authority who has their own board. If a customer can't go on and register for summer camps at the same time they pay their car taxes, we've lost a leverage opportunity. We of course have schools with their whole infrastructure and their whole system and separate logins and multiple different platforms. And I guess the question that I have for you is

Have you identified where this will be really difficult? And I should have mentioned the CSB earlier where you have, you know, confidential medical information, but people who think of the CSB think of it as just Fairfax County and we run it and we don't.

And so are you giving, are you predicting some of those anomalies that will be there? And are you building a system that maybe on day one doesn't envision accomplishing inclusion of all of those oddities? But in day 20, they can be added down the road.

Sure. That's a great question. From a strategic point of view, we really want to focus on early adopters in this first year, right? So build out some of the foundational aspects. I call it confidence building measures so that agencies can see what we're capable of doing.

The ones that want to be early adopters, they're going to help us get there, which then hopefully helps us create a great story for all the other agencies to work, you know, say, hey, we can do this. and we want to engage with IT now on it. And over the long term, I mean, this is going to be several years of work, and part of doing this work is going to be business process reengineering.

And being able to think, again, long term and strategically about those business processes are going to help us as we continue down this path. Part of what we can do around Six Sigma activities or, you know, other things where we're able to identify breaks in the process or holes in the process or things that are just extraneous parts of the process, we can prove that through customer interaction.

You know, we can prove that through those sort of design principles and then be able to share that, you know, with our partners and the agencies as well as the board so that hopefully we can break through some of those things. Yeah, I think that's important. And the early adopters, I think, are obvious. I would just say from a user experience, and you know this, what I'm getting ready to say, which is the more one can do with this account at the beginning is going to play a major role in how successful it's going to be.

So with the car tax one, maybe somebody searches once a year to find their password to go in there and do something, and that's the only time they use it. And so as these pieces get stacked on here, people's ability to go visit it will increase dramatically, and it will become known as the place to go.

If it starts out with just you can do one or two things, and it's a separate account for this department. And so I would just say as you're building it and reach those milestones, messaging out to the public and to us about, hey, this is the starting core of things you can do.

It's a lot more than you've ever been able to do with one login before. And we're going to be adding to this as the years go so that when a customer thinks about how they interact with Fairfax, they know to go here. Whether it's, you know, paying their car taxes, or I'm hoping we're even getting to a point where, you know, a customer is somebody who's trying to figure out how to get a permit to build their deck, that they can go log in one place and, you know, they'll be able to see their information more clearly, pay the fee for that at one place so that we don't have every agency collecting this and doing their own system.

And so I see great hope in this, both for customer satisfaction, our constituents, but so much efficiency that we can accomplish within the county. And that's why this is so worth it. Thank you. Supervisor Alcorn, did you go first?

All right. Thank you. Yeah, I'm going to pile on a little bit. I appreciate both the chair's comments. I guess I do have one question. This is great. This is – I love the customer focus. I think it's going to do great things, ultimately, on the business process side on efficiency as well.

I guess one question I'm looking at Tony over there and wondering if maybe this could help lead to a direction that I know we've talked about on the board. We have a number of different programs that have income qualifications. And I realize a lot of that is on the back end.

You know, it's not the front end. But is this a step towards that customer focus as well? So if you qualify for one program, you could qualify for others. Is this a step in that direction also? I think with the way technology is moving from a data and AI perspective, machine learning perspective, we can absolutely build that kind of intelligence into the platform.

I think it's critical. We've talked about this on the health and human services side. you know, and again, even it'll happen with the park side as well, and I think in other areas too, that being able to build in that intelligence and have the system know through Gen AI what to ask next, right? There's not, it doesn't necessarily have to be something sequential. It can be something that is, you know, bigger than that. It could be, it may seem a little disjointed from a data perspective or from a question perspective, but if we're able to understand what questions should be asked next and then building that into the

platform. And we can learn over time. So as we get more customers to engage in a particular product that we're offering, a particular process, the systems are going to continue to learn how one customer has asked about this and then takes information from the next customer and you're building that over time as you get thousands of different transactions that come into the platform. So short answer is yes.

Well, thank you for that explanation because it does help provide, build that out as well. And let me add on to that as well. I think one of the things that we talked about at the beginning is that confidentiality, the PII, the confidence building, right? So the data lake is going to be our data, first of all. So there's confidence that and the way that we're interacting with it is with Fairfax and nothing else. But we also want to be to ensure that we're meeting all of the compliance standards, and so we're not taking anything that's going to expose people to any kind of sensitive data being released into any other streams of operations and processes. So that's the, it seems simple, but it's going to be a little bit more complex, but we want to ensure that all of our customers recognize that we're going to keep all of the

same standards that we've held for years, but we're just going to allow their experience to be a little bit more robust as we move forward, and that we all feel confident that we're able to navigate breaking down barriers, but still keeping up the tight silos in terms of outside entities or compliance and sensitivity not being compromised at all.

And having a portal allows us to segregate the data so Supervisor Stork won't see what Supervisor Alcorn sees. And as Matt stated, building the generative AI on the specific as well as the other helps us collect data so we can move forward together.

And this approach should help as well. I know some of the data we collect are highly regulated by the feds, for example. Their federal programs are federally funded. So this approach would accommodate that. Is that right? That's the idea. Yeah. So within the data side of this, that data can be segregated however we need it to be.

If there are certain regulations around it, certain restrictions, if we need to block certain pieces of data or mask it from a presentation layer, from the user interface perspective, That absolutely can be done. We've been doing that kind of thing for years.

So from a technical perspective, it's pretty straightforward. Okay, very good. All right, thank you. To add to that, we also, I mean, we've been doing a lot of work with that stakeholder and stakeholder engagement. So the work that we've done and the conversations that we've had in previous efforts with the county attorney's office have really set that foundation level so that as we move into more predictive work, the analytics, the portals that we've talked about, The foundation of the policy is also there.

Rodney. Thank you. I think I heard you say business process reengineering and BPR. I had the opportunity many, many years ago to work on the CSP model. And as a part of it, there was the technical analysis, the social analysis, and the business analysis.

As I remember, with the business analysis, you're talking to your customers and really trying to get the feedback and input from them in terms of how to build out the system. So talk to me a little bit about the BPR process here and how it's being implemented to create this new model, which I'm going to say is also amazing that we're at a place now where we're even talking about this, and I think it's going to make a big difference in the use and quality of our residents' lives.

So thank you. Sure, absolutely. So this is an area I like to get low tech because it's, and this is true, taking sticky notes, putting them on a wall with the different steps in a particular process, and really evaluating each one of those steps independently of the other to really determine, is this something we have to do?

Is this a piece of data we absolutely have to collect? Why? You know, this is a challenging, you know, set of questions for the owners of the process. You know, we do it internally when it comes to, like, let's say we have an outage. We have a process called the five whys.

I mean, you probably have heard of that. It's an industry thing. And when we look at something that happened within the problem, we dig as deep as we possibly can, keep asking why, why, why, why, why. and then you're able to distill that into the thing that's the most important.

Same thing happens on business process, and that's where we want to get to. You want to simplify that as much as you can. Customers don't care about what our internal processes are and the complexities that we've built around them. So we need to strip that down as much as we possibly can.

And some of this we can do through technology. We can utilize some tools out there that can observe customer behavior. present different options to customers, whether it be language or the next step in a process, and find which one they choose. And we could put 10 of these into production at the same time, and then you pick the one that wins. So you're using data from the customers actually engaging with it to determine what that next step can be. So there's a lot of different ways we can approach it, but we're never going to be successful unless we distill that down to

you know the real critical components and then last if I could ask about the the worker obviously those employees and the departments and agencies are going to be melded to create this new process we have to help them understand this isn't necessarily going to remove them from employment right we've got to have them feel comfortable with the development of this as a way to help them do their jobs better I guess absolutely this is Brian and I have talked oh sorry

Yeah, I'm sorry. I was just going to interject quickly that we look at this, and I think we had IPAC about a year ago, and I believe I stated this is a workforce augmentation. It's not a workforce reduction. So it's going to be a lot of skilled training, upskilling, redoing, doing new things.

And, you know, with the help of the Deputy County Executive Seard as well as our new CIO, we're looking at new ways to engage our staff. But with collective bargaining, I'm going to have to kind of work that mix into it as well because I can't just go forward with anything.

I'm going to have to lay out a plan. We are going to have to lay out a plan. The Board of Supervisors is going to have to get behind the plan so we can go forward with the negotiations to ensure that we can have everybody move forward. That's the absolute right point. And, you know, if a worker can handle five cases today, when we build out this kind of technology, now they can handle 15.

So to the chairman's comment earlier, the efficiency gains are substantial, and you provide a better customer experience at the same time. Those are the goals. Yeah, that's the point I'm making is we just don't want people to be fearful of this change.

And the way we communicate it and the way we interact with them is going to be critical in breaking down that fear. Thank you. Great point. Thank you. And the training is a big component of that, too, because it's famously said by some AI professional, you're not going to get replaced by AI.

The job will go to somebody who knows how to use AI, which is really what the goal here is, the 5 to 15. Anyway, any more questions down on the end? I think with that, we're going to go to the next session, which is the food and beverage tax overview.

Is that going to Jay? Yes, sir. Good afternoon, Mr. Chairman, Supervisor Herity, members of the board. My name is Jay Doshi. I serve as director of tax administration. As you know, the board approved a food and beverage tax effective January 1 of 2026.
The tax will apply to food, prepared food, and beverages that are sold as a meal. The tax rate is 4% and will apply to the total cost of food and beverages that are sold as part of a meal.
And we have embarked on a journey to have our first 100% online back-end solution to support the collection, the reporting, and administration of this tax. We have been working very hard on this.

A huge thanks to teams from DTA, OPA, the county attorney's office, and DIT that have worked extensively now on this project. And our goal is to have, in time, a portal to register, file, and pay online, and to have a module that works with the other pre-existing taxes that these customers are subject to, such as a business professional occupational license or a business personal property tax

system. We have been embarking on a substantial outreach plan to include workshops, another one coming up December the 8th online, one more final one in January, outreach through business organizations chambers of commerce and the like which is critical the next step will be board offices and general outreach to the consumers and all of this intended to ensure that we do our very best to ensure that no one is left behind no one does not know that the tax has come into place

we have sent directly and i have additional copies should you need them they will go to the board offices as well. We have a guideline document that lays out the specifics of the tax, and we have it translated in six different additional languages, and it is all available on our website in an easy-to-access format. So with that, I'll pass it on to Rob, who will talk to you a little more about the technical solution. Thank you, Jay. Good afternoon. I'm Robert Barr.

I'm the IT program director of Revenue Systems Branch. We're closely with Jay and his team to ensure we're meeting the capabilities of the Department of Tax Administration. So this project has been a very robust project. A dedicated team of project managers, business analysts, developers, attorneys, public information officers, and testers have been diligently working to deliver a solution that will support the business needs, a communication package that will reach out to the community and meet the internal operational needs of the Department of Tax Administration as well.

In this project, we utilize an agile methodology, which encompassed of a 14-month plan from end to end with the termination of the actual project not being done until later next year. This was a cloud-first initiative.

As you can see, we want to take a step back. We had about 34 sprints total in this whole package. That means sprints are two weeks long, so you're looking at about 68 weeks of development and work as far as that goes, and about 1,100 tasks throughout the whole process. And this was all developed in-house, which is a great process for us.

It's exciting to me to see it come alive and build upon our technologies that we have, such as this being a cloud-first initiative. We merged two project plans with this. As part of the tax modernization project, we had put in a cloud-first initiative for all future implementations for the Department of Tax Administration.

We will be moving our current personal property B-POL system to a cloud-elastic environment, which should ensure better uptimes, more accessibility, and a more robust solution for that going forward. It's also built on our framework, which is known as TAPS, or the Tax Application Business System, which will allow us to utilize and reutilize code and modernize standards across the board.

Additionally, we work closely with our partner in DTA to ensure both a great internal and external system, making sure the user experience externally is easy flows appropriately and it also includes a real-time interface for both register file and pay and changes to the person's accounts this will allow for transactions to be all in one session which currently is not the way we do business usually we usually have a approval step in between so we've now accelerated that to be all in one shop it also removes some older processes and streamlined some of our other

business processes to allow for a smoother process in the back end, removing overlapping procedures that were done. And as part of the project, we're also deploying advanced security features to once again protect that PII that's very important to protect for our constituents.

And the good part about that is most of these features will in the near future be rolled out in our other online platforms as we move forward with updating those. This was a multi-agency team with an integrated solution for not only DIT teams involved, such as GIS and PLUS, but teams that are across the DTA area also working with county attorney and OPA for a communication package. But it also was working with other county agencies to obtain data, especially the health department for these current restaurants that exist. So it's been a very large

effort across the board. So looking at where we are, we're excited to say that we're on track. We're going to meet our go-live date of January 2nd for the external portion of things, but we have two major milestones as part of this project. The first is going to be the move through the cloud and releasing it internally so our staff and DTA are able to get out there and see and get look and feel of the actual solution and also support businesses that have questions. Additionally,

we're going to be rolling out the next phase of that, which is the external portion on January 2nd, which will be the major milestone because that's when people are going to be able to get in and actually see how this works. So we anticipate a lot of questions. So we are going to be ramping up appropriately for that as the first billing cycle approaches, which is February 20th, which we also anticipate a lot of questions, as this will be the first time people will be actually doing this tax. So we are prepared and ready to go. Additionally, we are always looking forward. In an agile project, you always create a backlog of nice-to-haves or items that may not

need to be done. So in the first few months, we're going to be enhancing the system. We're going to be getting rid of more of the other processes that take overnight or rely on different system some interactions, making things more real-time, integrating with other areas as well. And we're going to be re-architecting the solution as well to ensure that it's robust and able to handle any load that we get around that.

So as we move forward, we look forward to the challenge of accepting this new tax. And with the support of both DTA and other teams, I feel this project has been very successful and is moving forward well. And do we have any questions?

Okay. With that, I'm going to ask two real quick ones. I think they're real quick. And you may not have the answer. Do we have a feel for how many of our restaurant owners, et cetera, this will be their first time dealing with the meals tax versus a chain restaurant that is used to it?

I mean, I'm sure McDonald's and et cetera can just roll a system out. But do we have a kind of a percentage feel there? I don't, Mr. Chairman. Nationwide, it appears in terms of number of locations, you might be in that 30% range for the chain versus 70% for non-chain.

So that's a very high-level estimate and may not apply to us. So it's probably the majority we'll be dealing with at the first time. Yeah, you've got over 1,800 restaurants in Fairfax County that are not associated with Wegmans or Harris Teeter or whatever sundry supermarkets.

So if you use Jay's number, you take out a 400, So you're looking at at least 1,200 restaurants potentially that don't have facts. It's big. I think that's important because if it's the Harris Teeters or whatever, they're just going to roll out what they've already got developed.

And that brings me kind of to my second question, and I understand there was some industry questions about how some other jurisdictions are treating the beverage piece when it's beverage alone versus food and beverage. and I'm more interested in not necessarily the interpretation, but why is there a difference between some and others?

Sure thing. So I'll take a crack, and I see that Corinne Rockett, our deputy county attorney, has also taken a seat. This stems from the fact that the enabling legislation in the Code of Virginia is different for cities and towns versus the counties.

So we have one section of the code 581-3833 that applies to counties and 581-3840 that applies to cities and towns. It absolutely creates confusion. We flagged this for you in March when we joked about the fact that Christina Jackson's chai, if purchased alone, would not be subject to a food and beverage tax in Fairfax County, but the identical item would be subject to a meal stacks in Fairfax City if she were to buy one.

So we do believe that there's an opportunity to harmonize these provisions and to make it easier for the small and multi-location businesses alike. Very good answer. Do you have anything you want to add? Or did Jay cover the legality?

He did an amazing job, so I don't have anything to add. I think he's been well coached. All right, with that, I'll turn it over to the chairman. Yeah, I brought this up before, and I just want to get reassurance on this. Because it's a Virginia locality issue, the debacle that Richmond had implementing and collecting their meals tax, we've studied that hard and are confident we don't potentially have some pieces of the same problem with our own rollout and implementation.

And the reason I bring it up is because it's a city, but it's also Virginia, and it was recent, and it didn't go well. Mr. Chairman, you're right. And that for a tax that in that city has been in existence for over 30 years. So I don't believe it was the initial rollout, but it was events thereafter and most importantly, lack of communication, outreach, and just the willingness to sit down and discuss differences when audits and other.

The nature of the beast is that there will be items that we will work on. There will be items where the industry may have one perspective, we may have a different one.
